readings.title: A rain garden beside the road
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood planted a rain garden to catch water from a paved street. The first design looked attractive but filled too quickly after heavy rain. The central difficulty was water overflowing toward a pedestrian path. The plan assumed rainfall would spread evenly, while a road drain directed most of it toward one end of the garden. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried observations during several storms. Volunteers watched where water entered and left, marked the deepest areas and asked maintenance staff about blocked drains. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed one entrance carried most of the flow. Plants alone could not solve a problem caused by the shape of the inlet and the level of the nearby pavement. In response, the group adopted a wider inlet and raised path edge. Engineers changed the entrance and protected the walkway, then monitored whether the next storms followed the expected route. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: green spaces still require careful engineering. The garden could help absorb rain only if water reached it safely and people could continue using the path. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a rain garden beside the road, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Reading river samples honestly
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A volunteer group collected river samples every month. A single clean result in spring prompted some members to announce that pollution had ended. The central difficulty was one sample being treated as a final answer. Water quality can change after rain or upstream work, so an isolated measurement could not show what happened across a season. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried repeated sampling at fixed locations. Volunteers used the same method each month, recorded rainfall and asked a qualified laboratory to examine uncertain results. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed readings varied after heavy rain. The pattern suggested that weather affected the measurements, though it did not identify every source of the changes. In response, the group adopted a report showing dates and uncertainty. The group published all readings with short explanations instead of selecting only the most encouraging number. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: environmental claims need patterns not single results. The volunteers could celebrate improvement while remaining honest about variation and the limits of their evidence. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in reading river samples honestly, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Explaining a summer water limit
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A small town introduced temporary watering limits during a dry summer. Residents understood the aim but found the original notice confusing. The central difficulty was rules that were hard to apply at home. The notice used official categories without saying whether a balcony planter or a shared courtyard counted as a garden. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a question-and-answer page with examples. Staff gathered common calls and asked several households to identify what they were allowed to do on a particular day. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed plain examples reduced calls about exceptions. People still wanted to know when restrictions would end, so clarity about individual tasks was only part of the problem. In response, the group adopted dated updates and a review point. The council revised examples and promised a public date for reconsidering the limits as supply conditions changed. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: public rules need usable examples and updates. A limit is easier to follow when people can connect its wording to an ordinary decision at home. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in explaining a summer water limit, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: Refilling bottles in a public park
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A park added two drinking-water stations to reduce single-use bottles. One station was popular, while the other was rarely used. The central difficulty was an overlooked station away from main routes. The quiet station was clean and working, yet most visitors did not pass it during a normal walk through the park. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried a map of walking routes and refill stops. Park staff watched where people entered, asked visitors where they expected water and counted use at each station. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed visibility mattered more than equipment quality. The least-used station supplied safe water but was hidden behind a building and missing from several park signs. In response, the group adopted better signs and a future entrance location. Workers added simple directions immediately and reserved a place near the busy entrance for the next station. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: a useful service must be easy to find. Installing equipment was only the first step; the park had to help visitors notice it at the right moment. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in refilling bottles in a public park, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A rain garden can help a street handle heavy showers, but plants alone cannot correct every design problem. In one neighbourhood, water from a road drain entered the garden at a single narrow point. During storms it flowed across a nearby path before much of it reached the soil. Volunteers watched several storms and marked where the water travelled. Engineers widened the entrance and protected the edge of the path. They then observed later rainfall to see whether the change worked. The garden still needed regular care, yet its success also depended on the shape of the ground. Environmental projects often require careful attention to ordinary physical details.

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a neighbourhood group proposing how to monitor a rain garden beside a road. Describe what volunteers could observe and when professional help would be needed.
writing.explanation: 范文说明安全观察、专业介入和后续复查。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Neighbours,
I suggest keeping a simple record of how the rain garden works during different storms. Volunteers could observe from a safe place and note where water enters, how long it remains, and whether it crosses the nearby path. Photographs taken from the same position might help us compare events, but no one should stand in traffic or deep water to collect them.
If the inlet repeatedly overflows, we should share the records with the council engineer. Changing drainage levels is skilled work and should not be done by volunteers. The group could continue caring for plants and reporting blocked litter screens. After professional changes are made, we should observe several more storms before claiming that the problem has been solved. A short public summary would explain what we learned.
Yours sincerely,
A volunteer
